Documentation must describe what the product actually does today, not what it used to do, is planned to do, or appears to do. Before merging a doc change, verify every claim against current behavior:

- Don't document broken or no-op features with a "currently has no effect" caveat — either fix the underlying code so the doc stays accurate, or remove the documented item entirely. A reader has no way to tell a "broken, will come back" caveat from a permanently dead option, and documenting a no-op invites misuse.
- Don't list options, fields, or event types the reference doesn't guarantee or that the implementation doesn't actually support. If a table claims to be exhaustive, make sure it is, or scope the claim down (e.g., "these are the types scripts typically need to act on" instead of "every line type").
- Use precise verbs that match enforcement strength. Say a system "supports" a control if it can be overridden locally, and reserve "enforces" for guarantees the system actually upholds without a workaround.
- Call out meaningful behavioral variants (e.g., two co-existing product builds, stable vs. nightly channels) rather than describing only the common case — and verify that any setting name, config key, or command you document is correct for every variant, not just the primary one.

Example: instead of
```
| `CLINE_HOOKS_DIR` | Additional hooks directory |
```
when the feature is currently non-functional, either remove the row or fix the feature — don't write "Has no effect in this release" and leave it in the table implying it's a supported, soon-to-return option.
